new_statements.quote: 5.2 Stress. Stress is non-phonemic since it occurs on the first syllable of words. With the occurrence of the transitional vocoid [ə], phonetically the stress comes on the second syllable, but phonemically it is only one syllable. [kə'lubaʔ] /klubak/ 'sweet potato' [tə'ᵐbi:] /tbi:/ 'an outsider'. Words of two or more syllables may have secondary stress on the final syllable, and in many of these cases the words can be identified as compound words. ['ŋʷagə'lu] /ŋʷaglu/ 'smoke' from ['ŋʷag] 'fire' and ['lu] 'smoke'; ['maᵑkə'non] /magnon/ 'forehead'; [bə'luᵐpə'kɔ:] /blubkɔ:/ 'rainbow' from [bə'luᵐp] 'snake' and ['kɔ:] 'web'.

new_statements.relation_note: Catalog record 'Patep, initial stress (an earlier compilation-2026-08-31) = fixed initial stress, which is exactly what this source states; the source adds that stress is non-phonemic, that polysyllables (often compounds) may take secondary stress on the final syllable, and the schwa caveat for initial clusters.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress is predictable (non-phonemic) and falls on the first syllable of the word. Where a word-initial consonant cluster is broken up phonetically by a transitional vocoid [ə], the stress is heard on the second phonetic syllable, but that schwa syllable is not counted phonemically, so the stressed syllable is still the first phonemic syllable.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Words of two or more syllables may carry secondary stress on the final syllable; in many such cases the word is a compound (e.g. 'smoke' from 'fire'+'smoke', 'rainbow' from 'snake'+'web').
new_statements.exceptions: Only the phonetic caveat with the transitional vocoid [ə] (stress phonetically on the second syllable, e.g. [kə'lubaʔ] /klubak/); no lexical exceptions are given.
new_statements.identity_note: Lauck & Adams 1975 is based on about 800 words collected in the village of Mahomba in 1972-73 (p. 71); Patep is described there as one of six groups of the Mumeng dialect chain in the Buang family, spoken by about 1,200 people in five villages along the Lae-Wau road, Morobe District. Lauck 1976 describes the same variety (Introduction, p. 5-6; Rosetta scan of the volume's introduction gives the same 1,200-speaker figure). No other dialect is described.

audit.reasoning: Quote verified verbatim at the stated section/page in the (re-downloaded) 1975 SIL phonemic statement; coding 'initial, fixed-dominant' matches it. The record had no copies we hold and no grade; both Patep phonology sources are now obtained by the project. The 1993 paper by the same author (Data Papers 40:132) refines rather than overturns: stress is fully predictable on the first full vowel, i.e. initial unless the first syllable is a neutralized Cə syllable, in which case surface stress is on the second syllable (1975 had treated that schwa as non-syllabic). Coding can stay initial/dominant, but the record should cite Lauck Vissering 1993 alongside 1975, fill the strength of the evidence, and add a caution/edge note that pretonic schwa syllables are skipped (stress = first full vowel); optional final secondary stress in compounds per 1975 p.115. No instrumental or later study of Patep/Mumeng prosody was found.

sources.quote: p.132: '8) Stress always occurs on the first full vowel in the word, i.e. either on the first syllable (when the vowel is not [ə]) or on the second syllable (when [ə] occurs in the first syllable).' Canonical morpheme (C1ə)(C2)V(C3)(a(ʔ)): stressed syllable optionally preceded by an unstressed Cə syllable and optionally followed by an unstressed a(ʔ) syllable. p.136: 'even though stress is now fully predictable (occurring on the first fully specified vowel), it can be considered as the primary conditioning factor...'; author nonetheless prefers marking stress in UR to break the schwa/stress ci
